Q: Compare contents of two files in Dreamweaver A:

Dreamweaver works quite well with Total Commander. Simply specify the path in DW, for example, C:\totalcmd\TOTALCMD64.EXE (in Preferences > File Compare), and in the Files window, select Compare with Remote for the selected file. Dreamweaver downloads the file, saves it in the _compareTemp directory of the current project, and opens Total Commander, displaying the created directory and the directory of the local file to be compared. Then, select both files in TC and choose the compare command. It's not a perfect solution, but at least the comparison results are great because Total Commander clearly visualizes the differences. For me it's a better solution than, for example, in WinSCP.

Q: SQL Server Express INSERT unique incremented number from SELECT on the same table by several users without creating duplicates A:

The short answer to your question is yes, SQL Server does suffer from race conditions, just like many other applications. This is quite simple to demonstrate with a single table. Take the overly simplified table:

CREATE TABLE dbo.MyTable (MyID int NOT NULL);
GO

Now take the following batch (don't run it let):

BEGIN TRANSACTION

IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
               FROM dbo.MyTable) BEGIN
    WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:10'; --To allow for a second batch being started between the EXISTS and the INSERT
    INSERT INTO dbo.MyTable (MyID) 
    VALUES(1);
END ELSE BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dbo.MyTable (MyID)
    SELECT TOP (1) MyID + 1
    FROM dbo.MyTable
    ORDER BY MyID DESC;
END;
COMMIT;
GO

SELECT *
FROM dbo.MyTable

If you open 2 query windows, and then run both the result you'll get from the SELECT will be:

MyID
1
1

Yes, that's right, two rows with an value of 1.

The truth of the matter is that you shouldn't be using a "home made" incrementing value, but instead should be letting SQL Server handle that. As has been mentioned in the comments (by me), don't try to have a different incrementing value for each product; this is going to cause you problems. Instead have an ascending value for the column; it doesn't matter if there are gaps in the values. If you truly need to ensure that there are no gaps, then you can use ROW_NUMBER in your SELECT; just make sure you never DELETE any rows from your table (you'll have the "soft delete".

One method would be to use an IDENTITY, which would look like this. Notice the CONSTRAINT at the end as well, that ensures that the ID has a value less that 100,000,000 (so must be 8 digits):

CREATE TABLE dbo.FactorySerial (FactorySerialID int NOT NULL IDENTITY CONSTRAINT PK_FactorySerial PRIMARY KEY,
                                Printed varchar(3) NOT NULL,
                                UniqueFullFactoryNumber varchar(30) NOT NULL,
                                -- etc...,
                                CONSTRAINT Chk_FactorySerial CHECK (FactorySerialID > 0 AND FactorySerialID < 100000000));

Do note that limiting your max ID value could be a problem if you have a lot of failed INSERTs, as every time you attempt an INSERT you use an IDENTITY, even if no row is inserted.

Alternatively you would use a SEQUENCE; this is more useful if you need to have the ascending value in different tables. I'll demonstrate this anyway, but I think IDENTITY is what you need here:

CREATE SEQUENCE dbo.FactorySerialID AS int
    START WITH 1
    INCREMENT BY 1;

CREATE TABLE dbo.FactorySerial (FactorySerialID int NOT NULL CONSTRAINT DF_FactorySerialID DEFAULT NEXT VALUE FOR dbo.FactorySerialID,
                                Printed varchar(3) NOT NULL,
                                UniqueFullFactoryNumber varchar(30) NOT NULL,
                                -- etc...,
                                CONSTRAINT PK_FactorySerial PRIMARY KEY (FactorySerialID),
                                CONSTRAINT Chk_FactorySerial CHECK (FactorySerialID > 0 AND FactorySerialID < 100000000));

Then, when you INSERT values into the table, you just omit the FactorySerialID column your insert INSERT clause:

INSERT INTO dbo.FactorySerial (Printed, UniqueFullFactoryNumber)
VALUES ('abc','xyz');
GO

As has been mentioned as well, your VB.Net code is wide open to injection attacks; you need to parametrise your statements. I will openly state that I haven't tested this; I don't have access to a VB.Net development environment and I haven't worked with the language in over a decade. It should, however, look something like this:

Dim strSql As String = "INSERT INTO dbo.INSERT INTO dbo.FactorySerial (Printed, UniqueFullFactoryNumber) VALUES (@Printed,@UniqueFullFactoryNumber);"

Using sqlConn As New SqlConnection(<Connection String Goes Here)
    sqlCmd As New SqlCommand(strSql, sqlConn)
   
    sqlCmd.Parameters.Add("@Printed", SqlDbType.VarChar, 3) = PrintedDefault 
    sqlCmd.Parameters.Add("@UniqueFullFactoryNumber", SqlDbType.VarChar, 50) = DummyBCR

    sqlCmd.ExecuteScalar()
End Using

This VB code, as stated, is untested.
